newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia adopting tough gene-food laws.
newsitem.headline: Australia adopting tough gene-food laws.

text.p: Battle lines are being drawn in Australia and New Zealand over an official proposal that they introduce the world's toughest standards in the burgeoning genetically modified food products industry.
The Australia New Zealand Food Authority (ANZFA), a bi-national body set up in mid-1996, is calling for public comment on a draft standard which has set off alarm bells in Australia's food industry.

The standard would ban all genetically derived food products unless specifically approved. It would also require all products which contain even the smallest amounts of genetically derived food products, if approved for sale, to be strictly labelled.

"Absolutely miniscule percentages would have to be labelled. Virtually everything on the supermarket shelf would have to be labelled. It's overkill," said Pam Saunders, spokeswoman for the Australian Food Council (AFC).
With new regulations likely to be introduced later this year, the battle's frontline has been a boatload of U.S. soybean imports, which arrived in Australia last December.
"The gene bean has landed! But Australian consumers are left in the dark," the Australian Consumers' Association (ACA), said in a statement.
ACA is now pressing for all products which contain genetically modified material to be individually approved and then labelled.
SOYBEAN FIRST BATTLEFRONT
The food council says the consumer association would put Australia out of line with regulations in the United States and Europe and make nonsense of labelling requirements.

More than 50 percent of processed food around the world contains has some kind of soybean derivatives. To require labelling of products with even miniscule genetic content "makes a bit of a nonsense out of it", Saunders said.
Genetically derived soybeans are the only product now on sale in Australia which would be affected by the proposed new code.

Australian soybean imports, at about 100,000 tonnes a year, are worth between about A$35 million and A$50 million, depending on price. The December shipment contained the first genetically derived U.S. soybeans from Monsanto Corp's Roundup Ready beans, which form about two percent of the U.S. crop.
But more genetically derived products are on the way.
Later this year, genetically modified cottonseed oil will be on sale or contained in other products on supermarket shelves.

Monsanto Corp, which produced the technology for both genetic soybean and cotton, is also working on new genetic crops, with corn, canola (rapeseed oil), sugar beet, tomatoes and potatos all under active genetic development.
Genetically produced U.S. corn (maize) is likely to be the third genetic product to reach Australia --- if allowed in.
GENE-FOOD SIDE EFFECTS

The ACA is concerned that without labelling, consumers have no way of knowing that genetically modified material is in their food. ANZFA assessment guidelines also state that consumer concern exists over potential nutritional, toxic and allergenic effects of introduced genes in food products.

Australia does not see itself as a world leader in regulating the industry, but is recognised as taking a different approach from the U.S. voluntary system and from the European Union, which is considering compulsory assessment.

Nevertheless Australia's proposed labelling requirements are more stringent than regulations in Europe, while its 12-month review process for changes to its Food Standards Code are also more stringent than European processes, said ANZFA.
Monsanto, which leads world gene technology development, politely supports the food industry stand.
Monsanto agreed with the ANZFA guidelines in principle but would be "offering some comments (on) specifics and detail", said Marion Sheers, regulatory manager for Monsanto Australia.
Battlelines appear to be narrowing on detail already.

The ACF is not disputing the first two of five proposed new ANZFA labelling guidelines, which require labelling when genetic foods or ingredients are not equivalent to conventional foods and when health implications are involved.
These requirements are in line with U.S. regulations.

ACF does not agree with a third proposed labelling guideline on ethical concerns over genetically-derived food components. It recognised, however, that this guideline was part of European requirements, the AFC's Saunders said.

But AFC rejects proposals four and five, which require labelling of products when any genetically modified living organisms are involved or when genetically modified ingredients make up more than five percent of the food at the time of manufacture.
These proposals would give Australia the toughest set of regulations in the world, Saunders said.
Cost is not the problem, but rather the potential for labelling to cause consumer alarm, deterring them from buying a product because they think something is wrong with it, she said.

If Australia adopted extremely strict labelling rules different from the rest of the world, foreign suppliers may abandon the market or, through not labelling products which contained small undetectable genetically derived material, gain an unfair advantage over labelled Australian products, she said.
The World Trade Organisation was expected to become involved if Australia did impose labelling codes which were stricter than the rest of the world, she added.
